Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

evil adjective and noun

morally bad, wicked; a harm

also wicked, wickedness, an evil, evils, evil-doer

classical

Cic. de Or. 2.297: improbī esse hominis et perfidiōsī (Lewis & Short)
Phaedr. 2.3.7
Traupman 159, 407

improbus, improba, improbum

declension

wicked, bad (of people and what they do)

The everyday prose word for a bad man, the opposite of probus; improbitās is wickedness. Without a moral sense it means shameless, relentless, beyond measure: labor improbus (Verg. G. 1.146), the relentless work that conquers all (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • malum, malī n. — an evil, a harm, a misfortune

    noun, second declension · classical · Cic. Lael. 10: nihil enim malī accidisse Scīpiōnī putō (Lewis & Short)

    The neuter of malus (see bad): anything bad that happens to someone, from a misfortune to a punishment. Not to be confused with mālum, an apple.

  • nefārius, nefāria, nefārium — abominable, heinous (of a crime or its doer)

    declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 2.51: homō nefārius et impius (Lewis & Short)

    From nefās (see wrong): stronger than improbus, what offends gods and men.

  • scelestus, scelesta, scelestum — wicked; as a term of abuse, you villain!

    declension · also used · classical · Ter. Eun. 4.4.41 (Lewis & Short): ō scelestum atque audācem hominem!

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; Cicero does not use it of persons)

    See criminal.

  • improbitās, improbitātis f. — wickedness, dishonesty

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Traupman 159, 407

    Lewis & Short: frequent and classical.

Examples

  • successus improbōrum plūrēs allicit

    the success of the wicked lures more of themPhaedr. 2.3.7

  • Paucōrum improbitās ūniversīs calamitās.

    the wickedness of a few is a disaster for everyonePubl. P 58

See also bad, wrong, criminal, crime, sin, vice.
